items.stem: Why are transcripts of spontaneous speech usually written without standard punctuation?

Because speech is organised in utterances, pauses and intonation, not written sentences
items.answer: Because speech is organised in utterances, pauses and intonation, not written sentences

items.stem: Read an extract from a descriptive piece, ‘The Storm’: ‘Then the storm broke. Thunder boomed and bellowed over the bay, rain battered the tin roofs like thrown gravel, and the wind whistled, whined and wailed through every crack in the shutters. And then, just as suddenly, silence: the soft sigh of the sea settling back to sleep.’ Analyse how phonological and prosodic features contribute to the meaning and effect of this text.
items.answer: Indicative content: ‘Thunder boomed and bellowed over the bay’ (plosive sounds): the repeated /b/ sounds are loud and forceful, recreating the thunder; ‘whistled, whined and wailed’ (alliteration): the /w/ sounds and onomatopoeic verbs mimic the rising, moaning wind; ‘the soft sigh of the sea settling back to sleep’ (sibilance): the hushed /s/ sounds contrast with the earlier plosives, creating calm after the storm; ‘Then the storm broke.’ (rhythm): the short, heavily stressed sentence gives an abrupt beat that marks the moment the storm begins; purpose: to describe a storm vividly.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (AO1 understanding and AO3 analysis of how meaning is shaped). Level 5 (9–10): insightful, sustained analysis of how a wide range of language features and structural choices shape meaning; precise, well-integrated quotation; perceptive about audience, purpose and context; fluent use of terminology; Level 4 (7–8): clear, developed analysis of a range of features with relevant quotation; effects explained in relation to audience and purpose; accurate terminology; Level 3 (5–6): some analysis of features with appropriate quotation; effects explained in general terms; some relevant terminology; Level 2 (3–4): identifies some features with limited comment on effect; some quotation; occasional terminology; Level 1 (1–2): mainly paraphrase or feature-spotting; little relevant comment on language. Indicative content: ‘Thunder boomed and bellowed over the bay’ (plosive sounds): the repeated /b/ sounds are loud and forceful, recreating the thunder; ‘whistled, whined and wailed’ (alliteration): the /w/ sounds and onomatopoeic verbs mimic the rising, moaning wind; ‘the soft sigh of the sea settling back to sleep’ (sibilance): the hushed /s/ sounds contrast with the earlier plosives, creating calm after the storm; ‘Then the storm broke.’ (rhythm): the short, heavily stressed sentence gives an abrupt beat that marks the moment the storm begins; purpose: to describe a storm vividly.

items.stem: Read Text B, a blog post by a resident, ‘My Year on the Roof’. ‘I’ll be honest: when the council asked for rooftop volunteers, I signed up mainly to get out of my flat. Twelve months later I have calloused hands, a slightly ridiculous number of chilli plants and – who knew? – actual friends. It isn’t all sunshine. The lift to the depot roof breaks constantly, the water tank leaked twice in August, and our tomatoes were demolished by pigeons. But on Saturday mornings, with the traffic grinding below and Mrs Okafor handing round her ginger tea, it feels like the only quiet place in the city. If you’re on the fence, come up and see. Bring gloves.’ With close reference to grammar and syntax, analyse how the writer creates a distinctive voice and engages the audience.

items.stem: Read Text B, a transcript of a radio phone-in in which the presenter (P) talks to a caller (C). (Transcription key: (.) micropause; (1) pause in seconds; // overlapping speech; CAPITALS = stressed word; [ ] non-verbal feature.) ‘P: and on line two we’ve got Samuel (.) morning Samuel C: morning (.) erm yeah I just wanted to say (.) I’m sick of being told to take shorter showers when // P: // right C: when the pipes on my street have been leaking for (1) three MONTHS P: three months (.) wow C: yeah you can literally see it (.) bubbling up by the bus stop (.) and nobody’s come P: so you’d say the authority’s (.) passing the buck a bit C: exactly (.) exactly that (.) fix your own leaks first you know P: fair point (.) we have asked them on to the show (.) let’s see if they turn up [laughs]’ Analyse three features of spontaneous speech in this text. Comment on what they reveal about the relationship between the speakers.
items.answer: ‘morning Samuel’ – phatic talk: the greeting builds friendly rapport and welcomes the caller on air rather than conveying information. ‘erm yeah I just wanted to say’ – filler: the filler and hedged opener show unplanned speech and the caller’s slight nervousness on air. ‘// right’ – overlap: the presenter’s overlapping ‘right’ is supportive back-channelling, encouraging the caller to continue.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks: up to 2 marks for each of the following, according to how fully it is developed and supported: ‘morning Samuel’ (phatic talk): the greeting builds friendly rapport and welcomes the caller on air rather than conveying information; ‘erm yeah I just wanted to say’ (filler): the filler and hedged opener show unplanned speech and the caller’s slight nervousness on air; ‘// right’ (overlap): the presenter’s overlapping ‘right’ is supportive back-channelling, encouraging the caller to continue; ‘three MONTHS’ (prosodic stress): the stressed word conveys the caller’s anger and makes the length of the delay the focus; ‘three months (.) wow’ (echoing): the presenter repeats the caller’s words to validate the complaint and emphasise it for listeners; ‘passing the buck a bit’ (reformulation): the presenter sums up the complaint in an idiom, framing it for listeners; ‘a bit’ softens the accusation; ‘exactly (.) exactly that’ (repetition): the repeated agreement shows the caller accepting the presenter’s summary; ‘[laughs]’ (implicature): the laugh implies doubt that the authority will appear, aligning the presenter with the caller without openly criticising; credit any other valid, supported point.

items.stem: Read Text A, a speech by a city councillor at a residents’ meeting launching a rooftop-garden scheme. ‘Friends, neighbours, fellow gardeners – thank you for coming out on such a wet evening. Look up when you leave tonight. Every flat roof you see is a field waiting to be planted. Last summer, the pilot garden on the bus depot grew four hundred kilos of vegetables, cooled the building below by three degrees and gave thirty families somewhere to meet. Imagine that on every block. Some say it is too expensive. I say we cannot afford not to. So I am asking you tonight: lend us your hands, your weekends and your stubbornness, and together we will turn this grey city green.’ Analyse how the writer uses grammar and syntax in this text. Refer to two examples and explain their effects.
items.answer: ‘Friends, neighbours, fellow gardeners’ – tricolon: the three-part address widens from personal to shared identity, flattering the audience as ‘gardeners’ before they have agreed to anything. ‘Look up when you leave tonight.’ – imperative: the command makes the audience imagine a physical action, making the vision immediate and personal.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘Friends, neighbours, fellow gardeners’ (tricolon): the three-part address widens from personal to shared identity, flattering the audience as ‘gardeners’ before they have agreed to anything; ‘Look up when you leave tonight.’ (imperative): the command makes the audience imagine a physical action, making the vision immediate and personal; ‘Some say it is too expensive. I say we cannot afford not to.’ (antithesis): the parallel ‘Some say … I say’ structure raises the objection only to overturn it, turning cost into a reason to act; ‘lend us your hands, your weekends and your stubbornness’ (tricolon): the list builds from the expected to the humorous ‘stubbornness’, flattering the audience’s determination and ending on a light note. Up to 1 mark for each accurate identification and up to 2 for each developed explanation of effect.

items.stem: A student was asked to write a blog post by a teenager about living with water restrictions. This is the student’s response: ‘Day nine of the hosepipe ban and my mum has started timing my showers. Four minutes. FOUR. I’m not saying it’s a human-rights issue, but it’s close. Joking aside, it’s weird seeing the park go brown. The fountain in the square has been switched off and the ducks look personally offended. I get it – the reservoirs are at 31 per cent. But maybe fix the leaky pipes first?’ Write a well-structured reflective commentary on this response. Organise it by choices or frameworks, support each point with quotation and explain each effect.
items.answer: Indicative content: overview of audience, purpose and form; paragraphs organised by framework or choice; ‘Day nine of the hosepipe ban’ (time marker as an opening): to give a diary-like immediacy and a personal angle; ‘Four minutes. FOUR.’ (minor sentences with capitals): to mimic exasperated speech and create comedy; ‘I’m not saying it’s a human-rights issue, but it’s close.’ (ironic hyperbole): to mock my own overreaction so readers laugh with me; ‘the ducks look personally offended’ (personification): to make the effects of the drought vivid and funny; ‘But maybe fix the leaky pipes first?’ (rhetorical question): to end with a pointed criticism in a casual tone; comparison with the stimulus where relevant; conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (AO3 analysis of own linguistic choices, with comparison where required). Level 5 (9–10): perceptive, precise analysis of specific choices of form, structure and language, each linked to audience and purpose with apt quotation from own writing; insightful comparison with the stimulus where required; Level 4 (7–8): clear analysis of a range of choices with relevant quotation and effects; comparison developed where required; Level 3 (5–6): some analysis of choices with some quotation; effects stated rather than explored; comparison partial; Level 2 (3–4): identifies a few choices; mostly narrates the writing process; little quotation; Level 1 (1–2): little analysis; general or irrelevant comment. Indicative content: overview of audience, purpose and form; paragraphs organised by framework or choice; ‘Day nine of the hosepipe ban’ (time marker as an opening): to give a diary-like immediacy and a personal angle; ‘Four minutes. FOUR.’ (minor sentences with capitals): to mimic exasperated speech and create comedy; ‘I’m not saying it’s a human-rights issue, but it’s close.’ (ironic hyperbole): to mock my own overreaction so readers laugh with me; ‘the ducks look personally offended’ (personification): to make the effects of the drought vivid and funny; ‘But maybe fix the leaky pipes first?’ (rhetorical question): to end with a pointed criticism in a casual tone; comparison with the stimulus where relevant; conclusion.

items.stem: Text A is a review from a city magazine’s food column; Text B is a promotional leaflet for the same night market, both on a night market. From Text A: (i) ‘Arrive hungry and leave your diet at home.’ (ii) ‘fold dumplings so fast their hands blur’. From Text B: (iii) ‘Follow us @harbournights’ (iv) ‘kids eat free before 7 pm on Sundays!’. Using these quotations, compare the two texts, focusing on the relationship with the audience.
items.answer: ‘Arrive hungry and leave your diet at home.’: imperative – the playful commands address the reader directly and set a humorous, indulgent tone. ‘fold dumplings so fast their hands blur’: hyperbole – the exaggeration creates a vivid image of skill and speed, making the stall seem like a spectacle. ‘Follow us @harbournights’: social media handle – the handle links print to social media, inviting an ongoing relationship with readers. ‘kids eat free before 7 pm on Sundays!’: exclamative – the exclamation highlights a family incentive and targets parents directly. Overall: Text A evaluates the market, including criticisms; Text B presents only positives to sell it.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks: up to 2 marks for each of the following, according to how fully it is developed and supported: ‘Arrive hungry and leave your diet at home.’ – imperative: the playful commands address the reader directly and set a humorous, indulgent tone; ‘fold dumplings so fast their hands blur’ – hyperbole: the exaggeration creates a vivid image of skill and speed, making the stall seem like a spectacle; ‘Follow us @harbournights’ – social media handle: the handle links print to social media, inviting an ongoing relationship with readers; ‘kids eat free before 7 pm on Sundays!’ – exclamative: the exclamation highlights a family incentive and targets parents directly; a comparative judgement, e.g. Text A evaluates the market, including criticisms; Text B presents only positives to sell it; credit any other valid, supported point. At least one mark must come from an explicit comparison.

items.stem: ‘Private cars should be banned from city centres.’ Write an argumentative essay giving your views. (600–900 words)
items.answer: Indicative content: a clear, sustained stance; logically sequenced, developed arguments; evidence and examples; rhetorical devices (ethos, pathos, logos, antithesis, tricolon); counter-arguments rebutted; a forceful conclusion; register suited to the form; accuracy.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (AO2 writing: content, structure, style and accuracy). Level 5 (9–10): highly effective, sophisticated writing for the purpose and audience; ambitious, precise vocabulary and a wide range of controlled structures; cohesive, deliberately shaped organisation; consistently accurate; Level 4 (7–8): effective writing with a clear sense of purpose and audience; a good range of vocabulary and structures; well organised; mostly accurate; Level 3 (5–6): generally clear writing appropriate to the task; some range of vocabulary and structures; organisation mostly secure; some errors; Level 2 (3–4): some sense of purpose; limited vocabulary and sentence variety; organisation uneven; errors sometimes affect meaning; Level 1 (1–2): little sense of purpose or audience; simple, repetitive expression; frequent errors. Indicative content: a clear, sustained stance; logically sequenced, developed arguments; evidence and examples; rhetorical devices (ethos, pathos, logos, antithesis, tricolon); counter-arguments rebutted; a forceful conclusion; register suited to the form; accuracy.

items.stem: Read Text B, a blog post by a resident, ‘My Year on the Roof’. ‘I’ll be honest: when the council asked for rooftop volunteers, I signed up mainly to get out of my flat. Twelve months later I have calloused hands, a slightly ridiculous number of chilli plants and – who knew? – actual friends. It isn’t all sunshine. The lift to the depot roof breaks constantly, the water tank leaked twice in August, and our tomatoes were demolished by pigeons. But on Saturday mornings, with the traffic grinding below and Mrs Okafor handing round her ginger tea, it feels like the only quiet place in the city. If you’re on the fence, come up and see. Bring gloves.’ Analyse how the text is structured. Comment on the opening (‘I’ll be honest: when the council asked for rooftop volunteers, I signed up mainly to get out of my flat’), the development and the ending (‘Bring gloves’).
items.answer: The opening establishes the blog post and engages other residents and general readers of a personal blog; the middle develops content (the writer joined mainly to get out of the flat; after a year the writer has made real friends); the ending is shaped to the purpose: to share a personal experience honestly and encourage others to join.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks: up to 2 marks for each of the following, according to how fully it is developed and supported: effect of the opening; how the middle develops or sequences ideas; effect of the ending; cohesive links or shifts in focus; link of structure to purpose; credit any other valid, supported point.

items.stem: Nadia writes this sentence in a style analysis: ‘There is a rhetorical question and some emotive language and a statistic.’ Explain why it would gain little credit and suggest how it could be improved.
items.answer: Feature-spotting: a list of techniques with no quotation or effect. Improved: The rhetorical question ‘The difference?’ creates a pause that sets up the ventilator as the answer, turning the reader’s sympathy into a sense that money can solve the problem.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 for each of the following up to the maximum: identifies the weakness (feature-spotting: a list of techniques with no quotation or effect); explains what analysis requires (precise quotation, effect in context); a valid improved version.

items.stem: For the task ‘Write a story about two strangers stranded together.’, write a paragraph (about 80 words) that uses foreshadowing and unreliable narrator. Then label where each technique appears.
items.answer: A paragraph using foreshadowing (a hint of what will happen later) and unreliable narrator (a narrator whose account cannot be fully trusted) accurately, with both labelled.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: effective use of foreshadowing; effective use of unreliable narrator; relevant to the task; controlled sentence structures and vocabulary; accurate labelling.

items.stem: What is meant by the ‘context of reception’?
options: The circumstances in which an audience reads, hears or views the text
The grammar of the first sentence
items.answer: The circumstances in which an audience reads, hears or views the text
items.markingKey: Reception = how, where and by whom the text is received.

items.stem: Read Text A, a transcript from a student podcast in which two presenters, Kenji (K) and Zara (Z), discuss a new ban on phones in school. (Transcription key: (.) micropause; (1) pause in seconds; // overlapping speech; CAPITALS = stressed word; [ ] non-verbal feature.) ‘K: so (.) the ban (.) week one (.) how are we feeling Z: honestly (.) I thought I’d hate it but (.) lunch is actually (.) louder now (.) like people TALK K: [laughs] people talk (.) shocking Z: no but seriously // K: // I know I know Z: there was this one boy who was (.) he was just playing cards with the year sevens (.) which (.) never would have happened before K: mm (.) I do miss checking the bus times though (.) that’s a genuine (.) problem isn’t it Z: true (.) true (.) they could put a screen up in the canteen or something’ With close reference to discourse and structure, analyse how the writer creates a distinctive voice and engages the audience.
items.answer: Indicative content: ‘honestly’ (discourse marker): signals a sincere, personal opinion and marks the start of Zara’s turn; ‘// I know I know’ (overlap): the overlapping reassurance shows cooperative, friendly talk rather than an attempt to take the floor; ‘who was (.) he was just’ (false start): the self-repair shows the speaker planning in real time; ‘that’s a genuine (.) problem isn’t it’ (tag question): the tag invites agreement, softening a criticism of the ban and passing the turn to Zara; ‘or something’ (vague language): the vague tag keeps the suggestion tentative and conversational; other relevant features: ‘so (.) the ban (.) week one’ (ellipsis); ‘like people TALK’ (prosodic stress); ‘[laughs] people talk (.) shocking’ (irony).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (AO1 understanding and AO3 analysis of how meaning is shaped). Level 5 (9–10): insightful, sustained analysis of how a wide range of language features and structural choices shape meaning; precise, well-integrated quotation; perceptive about audience, purpose and context; fluent use of terminology; Level 4 (7–8): clear, developed analysis of a range of features with relevant quotation; effects explained in relation to audience and purpose; accurate terminology; Level 3 (5–6): some analysis of features with appropriate quotation; effects explained in general terms; some relevant terminology; Level 2 (3–4): identifies some features with limited comment on effect; some quotation; occasional terminology; Level 1 (1–2): mainly paraphrase or feature-spotting; little relevant comment on language. Indicative content: ‘honestly’ (discourse marker): signals a sincere, personal opinion and marks the start of Zara’s turn; ‘// I know I know’ (overlap): the overlapping reassurance shows cooperative, friendly talk rather than an attempt to take the floor; ‘who was (.) he was just’ (false start): the self-repair shows the speaker planning in real time; ‘that’s a genuine (.) problem isn’t it’ (tag question): the tag invites agreement, softening a criticism of the ban and passing the turn to Zara; ‘or something’ (vague language): the vague tag keeps the suggestion tentative and conversational; other relevant features: ‘so (.) the ban (.) week one’ (ellipsis); ‘like people TALK’ (prosodic stress); ‘[laughs] people talk (.) shocking’ (irony).

items.stem: Read a transcript of part of a campaign speech (↗ = rising intonation; ↘ = falling intonation): ‘we will build (.) we will BUILD (.) homes that people can afford ↘ (2) and if they tell you it can’t be done ↗ (.) ask them (.) who DID it last time ↘ [applause]’ Analyse how the writer or speaker uses sound to create atmosphere or emphasis, referring also to other language features.
items.answer: Indicative content: ‘we will build (.) we will BUILD’ (prosodic stress): the repetition with stress on the second ‘BUILD’ intensifies the promise and invites applause; ‘homes that people can afford ↘’ (falling intonation): the fall signals certainty and closes the promise firmly; ‘it can’t be done ↗’ (rising intonation): the rise leaves the opponents’ claim hanging, as if questioning it, before the retort; ‘who DID it last time’ (prosodic stress): stress on ‘DID’ pointedly contrasts the speaker’s record with opponents’ doubts; purpose: to persuade and rouse supporters.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (AO1 understanding and AO3 analysis of how meaning is shaped). items.stem: Read Text A, a feature article in a regional newspaper about the closure of the Rialto cinema. ‘For ninety-two years the Rialto has been the place where this town fell in love – with film stars, with stories, and quite often with each other. On Sunday its velvet curtains will close for the last time. Inside, the carpet is threadbare and the seats creak like old ships, but the projectionist, Mr Farouk, still climbs the narrow stairs each evening as he has done since 1979. “People say streaming killed us,” he shrugs. “Maybe. But you cannot laugh with three hundred strangers on your sofa.” The building will become a car park.’ A student was asked to write a short tribute to a closing local shop for a community newsletter. This is the student’s response: “After forty-one years, Mendes Hardware will sell its last box of nails on Saturday. For generations of DIY disasters, Mr Mendes was the calm voice at the counter: ‘Ah, you need a washer, not a new tap.’ He knew every customer’s name and most of their mistakes. The shelves are emptying now, but the advice he gave away free will last longer than any of it. Thank you, Mr Mendes.” Compare three of the student’s choices with choices in the stimulus text, explaining the reasons for the similarities and differences.
items.answer: Both open with the length of service to show the place’s importance. Both quote the shopkeeper, but my quotation shows his helpfulness rather than his view of the closure. The stimulus ends bleakly with bathos; I end warmly with gratitude.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks: up to 2 marks for each of the following, according to how fully it is developed and supported: ‘After forty-one years’ v. ‘For ninety-two years’: both open with the length of service to show the place’s importance; “‘Ah, you need a washer, not a new tap.’” v. ‘“People say streaming killed us,”’: both quote the shopkeeper, but my quotation shows his helpfulness rather than his view of the closure; ‘Thank you, Mr Mendes.’ v. ‘The building will become a car park.’: the stimulus ends bleakly with bathos; I end warmly with gratitude; comparative connectives used; reasons linked to audience, form or purpose; credit any other valid, supported point.
